newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN DAIRY INDUSTRY WARNS ON TARIFFS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN DAIRY INDUSTRY WARNS ON TARIFFS.

text.p: The beleaguered South African dairy industry has expressed concern that government might cut tariffs on dairy products, opening the way for a flood of cheap and highly subsidised imports.
This, it fears, could signal the beginning of the end of the local dairy industry, at the cost of thousands of jobs.

The Board on Tariffs and Trade on Thursday confirmed that it was considering import tariffs on the dairy industry, which have been left unchanged since they were introduced in September 1993, but that it would be up to the ministers of agriculture and trade and industry to make the final decision.
The industry understands that a decision is due in three weeks' time.
Milk Board general manager Bertus de Jongh told Reuters that although tariff cuts might be in line with government's policy to reduce the price of basic foodstuffs, this had to be done with care.
The problem was that the industry was just getting back onto an even keel again after the damage caused by the flood of imports after import control was abolished in 1992.

Bonnita Holdings Ltd administration director Koos Theron said the competition caused by imports put the margins of dairy farmers and producers under pressure because they could not get price increases to match rising production costs.
Dairy farmers could not feed their cows properly, reducing milk output, and some even went out of business. As a result, a milk shortage developed, which spurred on even more imports.
"This turned around when the rand had its fairly dramatic devaluation last year and it became more expensive to import products," Theron said.
"We will get our first increased production in the coming summer but it will take another year for the full benefits to be realised," Theron said.

Higher prices to dairy farmers had put dairy product manufacturers such as Bonnita under pressure, as was highlighted in its recent year results when it reported a seven percent fall in attributable earnings.
This, in turn, put pressure on retail prices with retailers arguing that their margins, too, were being squeezed.
As a result, imports are starting to look attractive to retailers again because, even with the weaker rand and import duties, they could boost margins.
But Theron and De Jongh are worried that this could set the whole vicious cycle going once again, especially as prices to farmers might have to be cut to remain competitive.
"It is government policy not to protect inefficient industries, but we are the third lowest cost producer of milk in the world," he said.
"The problem is that we cannot compete with subsidised imports from the U.S. or European Union or from imports sold by the single channel marketing systems in New Zealand and Australia."

He said that South Africa's tariff reductions were already way ahead of its commitments under the World Trade Organisation's Uruguay Round while EU states were still lagging behind in making their cuts.
Any further drastic cut in South Africa could be disastrous.
"If they are not cut too severely, we can possibly live with it," Theron said.
"But the more you import, the more you will depress the local price and the more you will be forced to import and the more job opportunities are lost," he said.
-- Lynda Loxton Cape Town newsroom +27 21 25-2238
